title: Design strategies and elements of building envelope for urban acoustic environment
review_question: To conduct a systematic review of building design elements for better urban acoustic environment based on previous acoustical studies, and to derive building envelope design strategies from the building envelope design elements.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included articles focused on building envelopes' impact on urban acoustic environments. Excluded articles not related to acoustics, built environment, or outdoor acoustics; lacking information on urban morphology or outdoor acoustics improvement; or without objective measurements for quantitative synthesis. Studies were grouped into noise abatement and soundscape categories.

synthesis_conclusions: Geometric and material building envelope design elements can reduce outdoor noise levels.
Vegetation on building envelopes shows good performance in both noise abatement and soundscape improvement.
Multisensory design and integrated design strategies are crucial for improving urban acoustic environments.
Architects, acousticians, and urban planners should collaborate for effective urban acoustic environment design.
evidence_gaps: Lack of conclusive findings for aircraft, railway, and wind turbine noise due to small number of studies.
Acoustic studies lack sufficient supportive results and practical applications to be appropriately reflected in architectural design.
More realistic research is needed to reflect acoustic findings in actual architectural design.
Soundscape improvement cannot be quantitatively identified.
Single-domain knowledge is insufficient for multisensory design strategies and processes.
heterogeneity_sources: Differences in noise levels between untreated and treated building envelopes
Variations in research methodologies (field, laboratory, scale-model, prediction)
Different noise sources (traffic, aircraft, railway, wind turbine, leisure)
Receiver's location (directly exposed canyon, shielded canyon, courtyard)
limitations: Small number of studies for aircraft, railway, and wind turbine noise, preventing conclusive findings.
Acoustic studies lack sufficient practical applications for architectural design.
Difficulty in quantitatively identifying soundscape improvement.
Single-domain knowledge is insufficient for multisensory design strategies.
